Because latent state paths are hidden, we use action-sequence alignment as an observable proxy for compatibility and instantiate it with longest common subsequence (LCS), which identifies a shared ordered backbone of actions while allowing recoverable detours. This perspective makes trajectory compatibility the central criterion for reference selection in multi-turn OPD. Experiments on ALFWorld and the airline domain of $τ^3$-bench show that LCS is the only evaluated reference selector to improve over reference-free OPD on both ALFWorld overall scores and all three airline metrics. Without further optimization, the airline-trained models also transfer to the retail domain, where LCS improves all three metrics.

title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games
summary: As large language models become more capable agents, they can exhibit deceptive behaviors, cheating human for higher rewards while appearing helpful. We attribute this failure to evaluation-side partial observability, where models are evaluated mainly from final outcome, without checking the faithfulness of underlying reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects. Prior mitigations address this partial observability by predefined evaluator latent belief space or one-shot monitoring, which do not extend to free-form language space and vulnerable to stronger deceptions that evade simple monitoring. In this work, we formulate deception mitigation as an Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Extensive Form Game (e-PoG), a max-min framework in which an agent maximizes reward, a monitor minimizes the agent's payoff by exposing deception from the full interaction trajectory, and a fixed verifier validates the monitor's claims and converts them into penalties. We define the solution concept as a Subgame-Perfect Oversight Equilibrium (SPOE) between agent and monitor, and prove its existence in finite games. With a perfect verifier, every SPOE is faithful; with an imperfect verifier, the guarantee persists if verifier errors do not reverse the ranking of monitor actions. To achieve faithful SPOE, we derive a two-timescale policy gradient algorithm and enhance the pipeline empirically with NLI verification and deterministic checks. Experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B on Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop show that e-PoG mitigates multiple emergent deception modes, outperforming the strongest baselines by 26.0% in deception mitigation and by up to 39.8% in task success. These gains persist under weak-to-strong supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/Toyoid/deceptive-agent.

title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
summary: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.

title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
summary: Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort, from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have given rise to increasingly capable Auto Researchers, which can autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: Given comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI research? To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher-Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152 ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the research process.

title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading
summary: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.

title: CARE-PO: Controllable Tool-Call Efficiency for LLM Agents
summary: External tool calls are a major running cost of an LLM agent, while its training objectives align almost exclusively with task completion. In a step-level diagnosis of Qwen3.5 trajectories at two model sizes on GAIA, a long-horizon tool-use benchmark, we find that most contain removable calls, at a similar rate at both sizes. Some methods add an efficiency reward to the objective to reduce the call count, but introduce problems of their own: the anchor they price calls against is computed from the policy's own rollouts (e.g., the group's shortest correct rollout) and so moves with the policy; training can drift toward a collapsed policy that issues no tool call at all, a degeneracy seen in published reports and in our 27B baseline; and a training run delivers a single operating point, so the user cannot trade efficiency against capability. We present CARE-PO (Controllable Anchored Relative Efficiency Policy Optimization) to mitigate these problems. The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's own difficulty and fixed before training. Injecting a successful trajectory from the training data into each online GRPO rollout group and charging for evidence a trajectory never gathers ease the drift toward a collapsed call count. Shaping the cost curve by an effort tag in the prompt yields an efficiency and a capability operating point from a single training run. On GAIA, five of the six operating points across three model sizes improve on their base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result is size-dependent: at 27B and 4B success rate is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.

title: Joi-Bench-Task: Benchmarking Task Coordination in Full-duplex Voice Agents through Interactive Simulation
summary: Full-duplex voice agents enable natural, hands-free interaction, allowing users to refine requests, redirect ongoing work, and seek clarification while the agent is speaking. However, existing voice-agent benchmarks insufficiently isolate coordination between task execution and conversation. We introduce a benchmark that assesses this coordination by examining whether agents track what is being executed, what has been completed, what has been communicated, and what remains to be reported as the conversation evolves. We propose an interactive user simulator that introduces configurable interventions at designated timing in tool execution and spoken result delivery, supporting controllable and reproducible evaluation conditions. We evaluate five leading commercial voice agents along three dimensions: execution responsiveness, coordination under request changes, and coordination under interruptions. Agent evaluations reveal persistent coordination failures. Under request changes, the highest result completion rate is only 55%, indicating difficulty for current voice agents adapting to new requests while preserving earlier obligations. After user interruption, four of the five agents exhibit average information omission rates of at least 23%. These findings highlight task coordination as a central challenge for current voice agents in complex, evolving conversations.

title: CRAFT-AI: Capability and Requirement Alignment for Flexible Manufacturing through Agentic AI
summary: One of the fundamental needs for reaching resilient production infrastructure is flexible manufacturing, which requires translating changing production requirements into implementable system configurations. This paper introduces \textbf{CRAFT-AI}, an agentic AI approach combining natural language (NL) requirement interpretation, Asset Administration Shell (AAS)-based capability descriptions, and reusable engineering knowledge from existing manufacturing configurations. A tool-using AI agent matches requirements with available capabilities and reference implementations to generate manufacturing scenes and corresponding AAS instances. The approach is demonstrated using a Factory I/O prototype with twelve reference scenes and five illustrative manufacturing tasks of varying complexity, providing an initial feasibility assessment of the proposed AAS-enabled, system-level generative engineering approach. For the four valid user task descriptions, proper requirements, correct references to the relevant engineering knowledge, correct components and lastly a valid Factory I/O scene are generated. For the task with missing engineering knowledge and a wrong sensor selection, the user is informed about which requirements of the scene generation lack domain knowledge and also which sensor is not compatible with the selected raw material by the user with link to the related documentation. After fixing the task description, the correct scene is seamlessly generated. \textbf{CRAFT-AI} highlights the importance of safeguards for risk perception and communication in foundation model-driven solutions.

title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
summary: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

title: KKT-Perturbation-Aware Communication for Fully Distributed Online Convex Optimization with Nonseparable Coupling
summary: Nonseparable costs and coupled constraints in distributed online convex optimization often arise when system performance and operational constraints depend on the joint configuration of all agents and cannot be decomposed into individual contributions. Such nonseparability leads to fully distributed decision-making with challenging partial local information, where each agent evaluates its local primal-dual update using estimated global information via a local belief of the joint action and the shared Lagrange multiplier to be exchanged with neighbors. While the belief consensus established by prior works ensures no-regret learning, exchanging beliefs comprising full-dimensional primal and dual states at every round imposes a communication overhead that scales with both the joint decision dimension and the network size. Existing event-triggered schemes typically activate communication according to state variation or consensus error. Under nonseparable coupling, however, errors of equal magnitude can produce markedly different perturbations after passing through the KKT operator. We therefore propose a randomized KKT-perturbation-aware communication mechanism, where the triggering of each agent's primal and dual communication channels depends on their impact on the KKT operator. The proposed mechanism transfers the adaptive-sampling principle of coordinate descent from allocating computation across decision blocks to allocating communication across information channels: channels with larger estimated perturbations receive greater priority for refresh. Under standard regularity assumptions, the resulting algorithm achieves $O({T}^{2/3})$ expected static regret and $O({T}^{2/3})$ expected cumulative constraint violation. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved learning and constraint-enforcement performance per transmitted bit over belief consensus baselines.

title: An Open Implementation Flow for the Xilinx Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 that Runs in the Browser, Checked Byte for Byte Against ISE
summary: The author describes an open implementation flow, from HDL to a programmable bitstream, for the Xilinx Spartan-3E (XC3S100E to XC3S1200E) and Spartan-6 (XC6SLX16, XC6SLX45), devices that only the discontinued ISE 14.7 supports. The flow runs unchanged in a web browser or in Node.js: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with nextpnr's Himbaechel framework given Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 architectures generated from Silinx's own device descriptions, bit database and timing model, and Silinx's own bitstream writer. The bit database was built by black-box observation of ISE's documented XDL and bitgen tools, using codeword-batched experiments; the router is given only switches whose bits were measured, and the writer refuses a feature it has not measured. ISE is the oracle: for the same placed and routed design, the bitstream is byte-identical to the one bitgen writes and ISE's DRC is clean. Placement and routing were first done by an in-house annealer and PathFinder router, which nextpnr replaced once it matched them. On 67 open-source designs for the XC3S1200E, compared with ISE at the same optimisation goal (45 designs built by both), the flow uses 15% fewer slices and has 14% shorter critical paths at goal Area, 21% fewer slices and 8% shorter paths at Speed, and 20% fewer slices but 12% longer paths at Fast (geometric means). XST cannot read 15 of the designs. The flow is published as the npm package silinx-fpga (Apache-2.0).

title: A Physical Testbed for Self-Driving Laboratories: Comparing Bayesian and Agentic Optimization in a Minimal Closed-Loop Color Formulation Task
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate laboratory robotics and automation with AI-driven decision-making to close the design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycle. However, physical testbeds that combine off-the-shelf hardware and AI into a functioning closed-loop workflow remain in early stages of development, and their integration with commercial laboratory automation is comparatively less developed. In this work, we develop a physical testbed that assembles and integrates commercially available laboratory automation instruments and demonstrate continuous, closed-loop, autonomous operation over 24 cumulative hours of unattended experimentation. We validate this platform on a minimal closed-loop discovery task in which the system autonomously formulates aqueous dye mixtures to match a target absorbance spectrum. The system completed six independent campaigns, each consisting of 48 closed-loop iterations over approximately four hours. In every campaign, the system autonomously selected, dispensed, and measured each mixture, with an AI-driven decision-making algorithm determining subsequent formulations without human intervention. Using this testbed, we compared the performance of two AI-driven decision-making algorithms, traditional Bayesian optimization (BO) and an agentic approach, in selecting mixtures under a fixed total-volume constraint. The agentic optimizer matched target absorbance spectra using fewer iterations than BO, with reductions up to 52%, and converged on a solution for one target that BO failed to match within 48 iterations. These results demonstrate a reference physical platform for SDLs that can evaluate both established and emerging AI strategies, including large language model (LLM)-directed optimization, before their deployment in real-world applications where experiments may be costly and time-consuming to prepare.

title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
summary: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.

title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
summary: Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. We compare in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting, LLM detectors) with deterministic enforcement outside the model (four reference monitors of increasing strength), human approval and taint tracking, judged by one effect-based oracle independent of every defence in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. In an evaluation with real open-weights models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B; 156 attack episodes per defence and model), the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes behind the task-bound monitor, which admitted 1.3% and 7.7%; guardrail effects depended on the model (a prompt guardrail moved obedience from 67% to 65% and from 86% to 55%, spotlighting plus a detector to 12% and 0%) against static attacks. Simulation with an assumed model covers what no real run did: under the assumed erosion law a persistent adaptive attacker or a compromised model drives every guardrail stack to 100.0% attack success, whereas the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%; its residual (harm 0.69/10) falls by 62% under taint-triggered human review, and a human layer without a deterministic monitor fails against approval spamming unless each episode has a deterministic approval budget. Implementation quality matters: a naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1. The real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only, and the larger model's detector stack contradicts the assumed erosion law. Code, data, a two-rater oracle audit and a notebook for repeating the real-model evaluation are provided.

title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
summary:
Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors.
  Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management. Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks.
  Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision.
  Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.

title: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
summary: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

title: When Credit Turns Against Tools: Transition-Aware Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. We trace this degradation to three coupled mechanisms: (1) tool-token imbalance produces negative overall tool credit when incorrect trajectories contain more tool tokens per turn than correct ones; (2) aggregation amplification can further strengthen this negative signal as token-mean aggregation gives longer incorrect trajectories greater weight in policy updates; and (3) failure-driven retries prolong trajectories as models tend to call tools again after execution errors, extending potential negative credit to recovery attempts. To counter this suppression, we propose Transition-Aware Credit Assignment (TACA), which targets the transition from reasoning to tool use through supervision of both call initiation and generation. Specifically, TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens within each prompt group through a minimal uniform shift. Additionally, TACA guides tool-use decisions with Decision Contrast, comparing rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers to the same prompt. Through Supervised Replay, it reinforces tool-call generation using calls from previously sampled correct trajectories. Across models and tasks, TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training, raising mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TACA.

title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
summary: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.

title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
summary: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

title: LoMASA: A Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant with Confidence-Gated Delegation for B2B Quoting
summary: Frontline sales staff spend much of their day re-coordinating quotes after customers change quantities, ask for discounts or new payment terms, or costs move. We present LoMASA (Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant), a training-free multi-agent system that runs entirely on one desktop computer. A 35B mixture-of-experts model (System-1) makes each decision in a single forward pass and reads its confidence from the probabilities of the answer options. A 27B dense model (System-2) writes customer replies and escalation briefs and is consulted when System-1 is unsure. Code computes every price, margin and option, and hard pricing rules cannot be overridden. On a test split of 500 simulated episodes with 1512 decisions built from public supply-chain data, the salesperson has to decide only 19.5% of decisions: 38.0% are settled automatically, with a median latency of 2.67 seconds, and 42.5% are escalated to a manager by the hard rules. On the automatically settled decisions LoMASA is as accurate as a rule baseline (0.894 vs.\ 0.894) and makes fewer commitments whose margin later falls below the floor (2.61% vs 4.53%); the price is additional escalations to the manager. Option probabilities are well calibrated without any training, unlike confidence stated in words by the same model. We also report where the design does not help: the 27B model rarely changes a decision.

title: Replay Fidelity in LLM Agent Evaluation: Randomness, Hidden State, and Test Oracles in AppWorld
summary: Reproducibility in large language model (LLM) agent evaluation depends on replay fidelity: which parts of an execution trace are reconstructed, controlled, and compared. This matters for agent debugging, failure analysis, and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use. We audit all 71 unsuccessful executions in a fixed historical AppWorld corpus using 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts. Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases under printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta, and native-verdict/test-count checks; resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68. The 26-case gap contracts to four under database/oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Mechanism studies identify four materialized-state discrepancies despite matching outputs and verdicts. In one admitted endpoint pair, an identical API call yields matching responses but different row effects; common future Python RNG removes that deterministic difference in two paired repetitions. A separate JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls expose authentication/write differences, with missing repetitions retained. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring and infrastructure deviations. The contribution is a bounded empirical characterization of replay eligibility, hidden state, and test-oracle integration, without estimating debugger accuracy, repair gains, or method-ranking distortion.

title: Do Benign-Trained Hidden-State Probes Detect Tool Errors Under Adversarial Conditions?
summary: Although hidden-state probes efficiently monitor model operation, it remains unclear whether probes trained on benign tool use remain useful for detecting incorrect actions under adversarial conditions. In this research, we assess this problem from the perspective of operational tool-action correct- ness. we use four AgentDojo suites, four conditions, and three models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and GLM- 4.6V-Flash (9B). We perform a five-fold, task-grouped out-of-fold (OOF) evaluation for each model. We train step-specific logistic- regression probes only on benign and non-defended trajectories and evaluate them on held-out trajectories for benign, prompt- injection, system-override, and tool-poisoning conditions. We compare our hidden-state probe to mean tool-call-token entropy, negative mean tool-call-token log-probability, and self-consistency uncertainty. The paired tests highlight six significant differences after Holm correction. All of the tests involve Qwen2.5-14B- Instruct under the system-override condition, with all three scalar uncertainty metrics obtaining higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP) than the hidden-state probe. These results suggest that benign-trained hidden-state probes should not be assumed to reliably detect operational tool-action errors under adversarial conditions.

title: What Broke & Why: Practical Lessons from Reinforcement Learning Post-Training
summary:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important way to improve how language models reason, solve problems, and use tools. But getting it to work in practice is not always straightforward. Training can fail because a model receives no useful reward, learns to exploit the reward system, stops exploring, or appears to improve when the evaluation itself is misleading.
  In this book, we give a practical introduction to reinforcement learning post-training for language models, focusing on what works, what fails, and why. We begin with the foundations of post-training, explain GRPO and the training loop step by step, and then follow five training programs covering math reasoning, search agents, training stability, mixture-of-experts models, and software engineering tasks. Each program shows the problems encountered, the changes made, and the lessons learned.
  The book also examines what reinforcement learning actually changes inside a model. The remaining chapters provide a practical reference for reward design, evaluation, training tool-using agents, debugging common failures, reproducibility, rollout engines, and hardware. Written for researchers and practitioners working with open models, the book aims to help readers understand how to train models, recognize when something goes wrong, and decide what to try next.

title: The Limits of Information-Flow Control Enforcement for Agentic Systems
summary: Information-flow control (IFC) is a promising approach to enforce policy in agentic AI systems. However, IFC suffers from label creep, a phenomenon where monotonically increasing security labels propagate through a system and progressively limit its utility. Label creep in agentic AI systems can be mitigated using two major strategies: (1) improved system design and (2) label declassification. In this paper, we characterize how far system design alone can mitigate label creep in agentic systems. Specifically, we measure how system topology, scale, and agent composition affect utility loss and security enforcement cost proxies for conservative IFC enforcement in a stateful agentic system simulator. We develop a pipeline to systematically vary these features and measure their impacts on label propagation. Our results demonstrate strong associations between structural graph features and our IFC utility loss metric (up to a Spearman correlation $|ρ|$ of $0.96$) and show that system size and tool allocation substantially affect how labels propagate. These findings identify design choices to reduce IFC utility loss, but they also demonstrate that system design alone cannot fully prevent utility loss due to monotonic label propagation. This motivates the development of label declassification mechanisms that aid these design choices and diminish IFC utility cost.

title: Is Recursive Self-Improvement Safe?
summary: The phrase recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to the idea of an AI system designing and creating another, better AI system, which in turn designs and creates an even better one, and so on. While the idea has a long history, it has always been an abstract, futuristic idea -- until recently. Today's frontier AI has attained a set of abilities, including in programming, mathematics, research, tool use, and working coherently over extended periods of time, that make RSI seem plausible. AI companies are starting to pursue it, but many of the involved people are also expressing concerns, asking whether humanity should really set this in motion and under what conditions. I will discuss the situation, argue that we do not even have clear frameworks for thinking about the likely outcomes of RSI, and do a quick game-theoretic analysis of how to choose whether to initiate RSI when another party is making the same choice.

title: From Weapons to Events: Evaluating Evidential Support in Multimodal AI for Policing
summary: Computer vision (CV) for policing has centred on recognising objects such as seized weapons, while body-worn video (BWV) is still reviewed by people, with existing AI tools using only its audio. Multimodal video AI could make BWV review faster and cheaper. At the object level, we present the KnifeHunter dataset, developed with UK law enforcement, with over 25,000 images of 543 knife classes and a protocol reflecting investigative conditions, and KHNet, a retrieval architecture fusing local and global features, which with about 125,000 distractor images attains 85.7% and 63.4% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the medium and hard protocols. At the event level, we present an evaluation protocol for video understanding pipelines, which describe a video as events and a transcript, that scores transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation and unsupported events. Whether each event is supported by the recording is labelled by a judge validated against blinded human labels. We apply it to complete pipelines, three 2026 omni-modal models and our hybrid NarrativeBridge-PAL-GPT-5 pipeline, on UKBWV-27, a pilot stress-test set of 27 publicly released UK BWV recordings (118 minutes). On this set the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures, yet it leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances, and every pipeline degrades on recordings from edited releases, long recordings and noisy audio. We propose readiness levels separating assistive tasks from those requiring verification of every output.

title: Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?
summary: Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. Report generation is simulated on a large multi-modality report corpus, with the orchestrator given either a catalog of finding classes consolidated from the cleared devices, each available on the modalities it is cleared for, or an unlimited catalog in which any class can be requested, and planning either from the clinical indication or from the target report. Tool outputs are simulated from the reference report, so the comparison isolates tool availability and orchestration from tool error. With the cleared catalog and the indication alone, the orchestrator recovers under a third of the clinically actionable findings; recovery improves substantially with the unlimited catalog, and further when the plan is written from the target report. Attributing every missed finding to a cause shows that most are classes no cleared device offers for the study's modality, and that a third are classes or tools that were offered and not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to the unlimited catalog on held-out reports, whereas a smaller orchestrator with the unlimited catalog gives up the whole gain. Tool availability and effective orchestration are thus complementary constraints on comprehensive AI-assisted radiology reporting.

title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
summary: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
summary: Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control. “I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover. More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960. "When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust," said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic. Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI. This week we published our first Public Benefit Report [link], a public account of how we’re working toward our mission and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five mission pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. “Anthropic's Public Benefit Report sets out what we’re all working toward: helping the world build powerful AI safely, and making sure the technology drives advances that meaningfully improve people’s lives and society as a whole,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Both goals depend on a deep understanding of frontier science and leading with integrity. Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

title: Introducing new AI functions for AlloyDB: ai.classify and ai.extract
summary:
Transactional databases store vast amounts of unstructured text — clinical notes, customer reviews, support tickets, invoices, and property descriptions. Historically, working with this text meant building complex application code: You had to export data from the database, call external model endpoints, write custom prompt wrappers, parse unpredictable responses, manage retry logic, and update database records. This application-side loop creates operational friction. It introduces query latency, bloats application code, increases model token costs, and creates data compliance risks by moving sensitive information across multiple network boundaries.

We built AlloyDB AI to bring Gemini world knowledge directly into your operational database. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a disconnected external service, we integrated model intelligence directly into the database engine. Today, we are announcing the preview of two new SQL functions in the AlloyDB AI query engine — ai.classify and ai.extract — available in the google_ml_integration extension (version 1.6.1 or later) on PostgreSQL 18, allowing you to perform classification and structured extraction directly inside your database using standard SQL. Supported by smart batching for AI functions (previously known as AI Function Acceleration), these functions deliver production scalability and performance. 

Now, let’s take a look at these new functions and how to use them.

Classifying text directly in SQL with ai.classify

The ai.classify function categorizes text into user-defined classes without requiring manual prompt engineering. You can specify categories as a simple list of labels or provide a list containing label names and descriptions to guide model context.

Key capabilities include:

  • Single-label classification (output_mode => 'single') to assign the single best category

  • Multi-label classification (output_mode => 'multi') to return all matching categories

  • Category descriptions using 2D arrays to provide explicit context for each label

  • Few-shot prompting by supplying inline examples

  • Flexible execution modes for individual rows (TEXT), arrays (TEXT[]), and cursors (REFCURSOR)

Here’s a quick example showing how you can classify customer feedback directly within a SQL query:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SET google_ml_integration.enable_preview_ai_functions = TRUE;\r\n\r\nCREATE TABLE product_reviews (id INT, review TEXT);\r\n\r\nINSERT INTO product_reviews VALUES\r\n(1, 'Fantastic, would buy again!'),\r\n(2, 'Broken on arrival.'),\r\n(3, 'Mediocre, not worth the price.');\r\n\r\nSELECT unnest(\r\n ai.classify(\r\n inputs => ARRAY(SELECT review FROM product_reviews ORDER BY id),\r\n categories => ARRAY[\r\n ['positive', 'Good sentiment'],\r\n ['neutral', 'Neither good nor bad sentiment'],\r\n ['negative', 'Bad sentiment']\r\n ],\r\n batch_size => 5\r\n )\r\n) AS sentiment;\r\n\r\n-- Expected Output:\r\n-- sentiment\r\n-- ---------\r\n-- positive\r\n-- negative\r\n-- negative"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f15da12e310>)])]>

Extracting structured JSON with ai.extract

The ai.extract function transforms unstructured text into structured JSON data matching your target schema — specified as a JSON schema or a text list of fields. It handles system instructions internally, saving you from writing prompt templates or response parsers.

Key capabilities include:

  • Schema flexibility supporting standard JSON schemas or plain text field lists

  • Automatic transformation of unstructured text into machine-readable JSON

  • Overloaded function signatures for single rows, arrays, and cursor batching

Here’s an example extracting clinical fields from free-form medical notes:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'SET google_ml_integration.enable_preview_ai_functions = TRUE;\r\n\r\nSELECT ai.extract( \r\n input => \'Patient Jane Smith, 52 years old, visited the clinic on Oct 25. She is currently experiencing a mild fever, persistent cough, and severe body aches. The doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and Amoxicillin.\',\r\n output_schema => \'{\r\n "patient_name": {"type": "string"},\r\n "age": {"type": "integer"},\r\n "symptoms": {\r\n "type": "array",\r\n "items": {"type": "string"}\r\n },\r\n "prescribed_medications": {\r\n "type": "array",\r\n "items": {"type": "string"}\r\n }\r\n }\'\r\n);\r\n\r\n--- Expected output \r\n-- {\r\n-- "patient_name": "Jane Smith",\r\n-- "age": 52,\r\n-- "symptoms": [\r\n-- "mild fever",\r\n-- "persistent cough",\r\n-- "severe body aches"\r\n-- ],\r\n-- "prescribed_medications": [\r\n-- "Ibuprofen",\r\n-- "Amoxicillin"\r\n-- ]\r\n-- }'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f15e8cced10>)])]>

Speeding up queries with smart batching

Running AI evaluations row-by-row can slow down query execution. AlloyDB addresses this with smart batching for AI functions. When you use ai.classify or ai.extract in SQL WHERE clause expressions, the database engine automatically groups inputs into optimized micro-batches before sending them to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models.

Smart batching delivers significant performance and efficiency improvements:

  • Faster inference for query execution compared to row-at-a-time evaluations

  • Reduces total model token spend by optimizing input prompt overhead

Real-world industry applications

Native classification and extraction functions support operational workflows across key industry sectors:

  • Healthcare: Securely convert free-text clinical notes into structured records containing patient names, symptoms, and prescribed medications, keeping patient data safely within the confines of the database.

  • Financial services: Extract vendor details, invoice dates, and line-item totals from scanned document text.

  • Legal technology: Pull governing law, liability caps, and termination notice periods from contract documents.

  • Real estate: Extract property types, bedroom counts, and price ranges from descriptive listing text.

  • Knowledge graphs: Extract entities and relationships from documents to populate PostgreSQL Property Graph (PGQ) structures.

Next steps and getting started

We are continuing to expand in-database AI capabilities in AlloyDB, with upcoming enhancements planned for advanced cost optimization, line-level provenance tracking, and query pushdowns beyond WHERE clauses.

To start using ai.classify and ai.extract in your database:

  • Review the AlloyDB AI Query Engine documentation.

  • Explore the AlloyDB release notes.

title: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification
summary:
It just got easier to prove your expertise in building production-ready agents. Today, Google Cloud is introducing the Professional Agentic Architect certification as the latest milestone in our Gemini Agent Ready (GEAR) initiative. Nearly one million developers are using GEAR to skill up on agents, but what makes this particular certification so special is its adoption within Google’s walls.

Over the past four months, Google Cloud has trained thousands of forward deployed engineers and strategic partners on our own advanced curriculum. Originally built as an internal training initiative, we are now opening it up to the entire developer community and partner ecosystem through this new certification. 

As the VP who manages our forward-deployed engineers here at Google Cloud (Ravi) and the managing director of Google Cloud learning (Gary), we’ve seen just how effective this program has been inside Google at helping our teams rethink the way they build, deploy, and use AI in everyday in almost every way. We’re equally about what this new certification can bring to everyone — developers, engineers, and anyone else ready to demonstrate their agentic leadership.

A new hybrid format to validate your real-world skills

This is not a traditional multiple choice exam. Google has introduced a new hybrid format that requires you to prove both conceptual know-how and hands-on execution.

  1. Part 1 (The multiple choice proctored exam): Evaluates your system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance.

  2. Part 2 (Hands-on labs on Google Skills): Puts you in an active cloud environment to build, test, and debug live agentic workflows.

Why earning this certification can help advance your career

As enterprises look to find top AI talent, this certification immediately signals that you have the advanced skills necessary to design secure, governed, and high-performance multi-agent systems. 

Our research with Ipsos on AI skill building shows that certifications drive more recruiter outreach: 82% of learners using Google Skills say that mentioning Google Cloud certifications on their resume drives more recruiter responses.

And it’s not just about getting the call — it’s about being able to answer it. That same research showed that 90% of cloud professionals say credentials like Google Cloud certifications give them the verified know-how needed to fill in-demand roles. 

What’s covered on the exam

The certification validates your proficiency across five key domains:

  1. Build agents using low-code tools (democratizing rapid agent prototyping).

  2. Use coding agents for application development (supercharging your coding productivity).

  3. Develop custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks.

  4. Evaluate and deploy agentic workflows (monitoring, optimizing, and ensuring performance).

  5. Secure and govern agentic workflows (protecting sensitive enterprise data and ensuring model safety).

Battle-tested by thousands of Google Cloud engineers and partners — now available to you

Enterprise demand for agentic workloads has skyrocketed. As our customers move past AI prompting and run their most business critical workloads on Google Cloud, we’ve built our own team that delivers the agentic future with them — at scale. Google Cloud partners and Google’s forward deployed engineers are embedded directly with customers around the world and are prepared to solve deep technical challenges because of this rigorous curriculum and certification.

While building our forward-deployed engineering program, we wanted to standardize training and upskilling for customers, Google Cloud partners, and our own engineers with the Professional Agentic Architect certification. This ensures our own teams are using the same world-class standards that we recommend to our customers and partners, allowing us to learn from each other and sharpen our skills together. 

Skill up for your certification at no cost today

  1. Register for Gemini Agent Ready to get access to 35 free monthly learning credits on Google Skills. For Google Cloud customers, Get Certified provides a cohort-based, guided certification journey at no cost. 

  2. For Google Cloud partners, register for Partner Certification Kickstart and review the partner learning path.

  3. Review the exam guide, learning path and sample questions.

  4. Get hands-on with Google Skills labs and preparation modules to get comfortable developing custom agents on Gemini platform with open source frameworks. 

  5. Register for the multiple-choice exam, complete the hands-on lab requirements, and claim your digital badge to showcase your expertise to the world.

Don't just prompt AI — architect it. Get certified today.

title: Introducing Gemini for healthcare
summary:
Every healthcare organization is working to deliver great care to more people at a lower cost. However, a general AI model is not enough to solve this challenge. Today, healthcare runs on fragmented data. Patient records, coverage policies, and clinical evidence remain trapped across disconnected records, claims systems, and administrative tools that don’t work together. Clinicians are forced to spend nearly 28 hours a week on manually reconciling information, and patients wait for answers about their care and their coverage.

Healthcare organizations need a single, secure, governed orchestration layer that coordinates work across the systems they already run, assembling verifiable evidence and taking multi-step workflows through to completion with human oversight.

Today, we are announcing Gemini for healthcare. This purpose-built industry solution extends the universal Gemini agent, we introduced last month at Gemini at Work. 

The Gemini agent is a single, always-on agent for work where employees delegate an objective, and the agent plans the steps, retains organizational context, and routes across the best models to deliver finished outcomes inside the tools teams already use. The Gemini agent is built with enterprise-grade identity administration, fine-grained access control, and centralized policy management directly into its runtime. Every agent operates with a distinct identity, inherits each user’s existing role-based permissions, and enforces strict need-to-know boundaries across every user, sub-agent, and workflow. 

Working across clinical, financial, and administrative systems, it orchestrates multi-step tasks without forcing teams to switch applications:

  • For providers: Gemini provides a patient’s history across care settings, charts are prepared before the visit, and authorization packets are assembled against payer policy before submission, so fewer claims come back denied.

  • For health plans and payers: Gemini ensures requests are checked against medical policy and organized for the clinical reviewer, and benefits and costs are explained to members from their own plan documents.

Gemini for healthcare is built to support HIPAA compliance, with governance running underneath it all. It’s available starting today in preview.

Four components of Gemini for healthcare

Developed alongside clinical and health plan leaders, Gemini for healthcare provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for payers and providers with four core components:

  1. Skills for healthcare work: Skills are reusable instructions and context, written by domain experts, that teach Gemini to run a specific task. Purpose-built, multi-step instructions guide the Gemini agent through essential clinical and administrative tasks, such as medical records synthesis, pre-appointment preparation, coverage and policy review, and payer benefit determination. Each skill applies your organization’s policies and plan rules, and teams can build custom skills tailored to the workflows and standard operating procedures unique to their organization.

  2. Connectors to clinical, financial, and operational systems: A library of connectors links Gemini directly to the EHR, claims, care management, and administrative systems organizations already run. Gemini queries each system while strictly preserving existing identity and role-based access controls, so teams get unified context without migrating sensitive data or altering permissions.

  3. An open healthcare partner ecosystem: Every health system and health plan runs a different mix of systems. Healthcare systems integrators and digital health partners help organizations extend Gemini with specialized solutions, connect it to what they already run, and scale it without lock-in.

  4. A secure, governed platform with open model choice: Clinical, security, and IT leaders get one place to set and enforce policies that govern every agent interaction. It is built to support HIPAA compliance, with enterprise-grade access controls, end-to-end audit logging, and verifiable citations so reviewers can check where each answer came from. Because the agent supports model choice, organizations can pair frontier models from Google and leading partners for complex clinical reasoning with fast, cost-efficient models for routine administrative steps under the same governance.

Unlocking high-value workflows with skills designed for payers and providers

Gemini for healthcare takes on the heavy assembly and administrative work that slows down clinical decisions and coverage determinations. 

At the point of care:

  • Building a longitudinal timeline from fragmented sources:  Synthesizes EHR and external records, separates active problems from resolved ones, lists allergies, and flags medication discrepancies. Clinicians get a grounded and unified patient picture in minutes rather than piecing together history across disconnected systems.

  • Reclaiming preparation time between patients: Prepares the patient chart ahead of a scheduled visit or procedure, flagging interval events, current medications, and outstanding clearances, labs, or consents, so care teams walk in with the full picture.

  • Streamlining clinical authorization and appeals: Extracts relevant chart evidence into an audit-ready packet for review, aligned with payer policy, flagging documentation gaps before submission rather than after a denial. If denials do occur, and the record supports it, it drafts an appeal grounded directly in the clinical record and the plan’s policy.

At the point of coverage:

  • Accelerating payer review: Checks incoming requests against the health plan’s medical policies and organizes the findings for reviewers, with findings traceable to the submitted documentation and coverage policy. Clinical reviewers spend less time assembling files and more time applying professional judgment.

  • Demystifying benefits and patient financial liability: Parses complex plan benefit booklets to estimate out-of-pocket costs, track deductibles, and verify in-network status, giving member services staff a step-by-step breakdown grounded in the member’s actual plan documents. For Medicare Advantage members, it applies Medicare’s coverage criteria where a plan’s internal rule is stricter.

Open ecosystem of connectors across the healthcare tech stack

Gemini for healthcare connects directly to core clinical, operational, and industry systems via secure connectors, inheriting each source system’s existing role-based access controls and data permissions.

EHRs and clinical data integration:

  • Epic EHR: Gives authorized users read-only access to patient conditions, medications, labs, clinical notes, and specialist documentation. With no write-back to the underlying chart, clinical data integrity remains completely intact.
  • Oracle Health EHR: Surfaces read-only patient histories, diagnostics, lab results, and clinical documentation for authorized users while enforcing zero write-back to ensure data integrity for the system of record.
  • InterSystems FHIR Server: Extending beyond EHR integrations, InterSystems FHIR MCP Server provides standardized, high-performance FHIR repository management and clinical data interoperability.
  • Verato: Resolves patient identity and matches records across visits and sources.
  • Keragon - Healthcare Integrations: Provides connectivity to 400+ healthcare applications, including EHRs, enabling organizations to securely connect their existing healthcare systems through a single MCP integration.

Eligibility, claims, and pricing:

  • Optum Coordination of Benefits: Finds additional patient coverage and determines the correct order of benefits before billing. Currently in limited release and testing with Gemini for Healthcare. 
  • Optum Network Eligibility: Retrieves patient eligibility and benefit details from connected health plans in real time. Currently in limited release and testing with Gemini for Healthcare.
  • TriZetto Provider Solutions: Verifies patient eligibility, coverage, co-pays, and deductibles across Medicare, Medicaid, and major commercial plans via TriZetto's vast network.
  • GoodRx: Enables care teams to discover prescription pricing and savings options, including manufacturer-sponsored self-pay programs, directly within AI-powered workflows to help patients access more affordable medications.
  • Infinitus Relay: Automates high-volume payer phone calls required for prior authorization and benefit verification.

Terminology and coding:

  • IMO Health: Brings terminology normalization, clinical search, and knowledge graphs into healthcare skills and governed agentic workflows.
  • ICD-10 Codes: Searches and validates ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes, billable status, and hierarchy.
  • RxNorm Drug Vocabulary: Looks up standardized drug names, ingredients, strengths, dose forms, and NDCs.

Coverage and provider reference:

  • CMS Coverage: Connects directly to Medicare coverage rules, National and Local Coverage Determinations (NCDs/LCDs), ensuring coverage reasoning rests on current published policy rather than static model knowledge.
  • NPPES NPI Registry: Verifies provider identity, clinical taxonomy, and practice location in real time.

Evidence based guidelines:

  • Optum EvidenceVue: Turns real-world clinical data into actionable evidence through AI-powered workflows from Optum Life Sciences. 
  • BMJ Digital Health: Delivers expert-curated, structured, peer-reviewed clinical guidelines and evidence, grounding care and coverage decisions in verifiable citations.

Clinical and operational workflows:

  • Salesforce: Headless Salesforce Health Cloud integrations bring workflows, data models, and Agentforce into Gemini for governed action right in the flow of work.
  • Suki: Delivers Ambient Clinical Intelligence across healthcare workflows, transforming clinical conversations into actionable intelligence that powers documentation, coding, revenue cycle management, and clinical reasoning.
  • UiPath: Connects healthcare-ready UiPath automations and agents to help teams assemble citation-backed context for operational reviews, prior authorizations, and appeals.
  • Synthpop Careflow: Orchestrates the patient journey across referral intake, coverage verification, and patient follow-up, turning unstructured referrals into validated, payer-ready orders without manual re-entry.
  • Alteryx: Enables healthcare teams to turn their domain expertise into automated analytics workflows, grounding AI-driven insights in business rules and calculations that are visible, understandable, repeatable, and auditable.

Enterprise productivity and collaboration:

  • Sana from Workday: Connects HR, finance, and enterprise knowledge so healthcare teams can surface policies, coordinate tasks, and get work done across administrative systems.
  • ServiceNow: Tracks IT incidents, operational service requests, and approval chains while enforcing existing enterprise routing rules.
  • Microsoft 365: Integrates directly with Word, Outlook, and SharePoint so prepared authorization packets, appeal letters, and benefit breakdowns land directly in the tools where teams already work.
  • Google Workspace: Connects seamlessly with Google Docs, Gmail, Drive, and Sheets to surface internal files and coordinate administrative workflows while enforcing enterprise access controls.

Security and compliance:

  • Cyera Dataport: Integrates with Cyera for data and agent security, delivering protected health information (PHI) context to support HIPAA audits and compliance reporting.

Global implementation partners and ecosystem

Through our open platform, organizations can deploy specialized partner agents such as ASCO Oncology Guideline Assistant or work with healthcare systems integrators, including 66degrees, Accenture, Altimetrik, AuxoAI, Cognizant, Deloitte, Egen, HCLTech, KPMG, NTT DATA, PwC, Quantiphi, Slalom, Tata Consultancy Services, TEKsystems Global Services, and Wipro, to customize, integrate, and scale these capabilities across complex enterprise architectures without vendor lock-in.

Developed alongside leading healthcare organizations

Health systems, health plan providers, academic medical centers, and clinical leaders are already working with Google Cloud to shape and apply these capabilities across care delivery, plan operations, and medical research: 

Synthesizing patient context at the point of care

  • “Making it easier for physicians to access and understand a patient’s medical history helps them spend less time gathering information and more time focused on patient care. Through our work with Google Cloud, we’re exploring how Gemini can interpret and synthesize complex patient information from multiple electronic health record systems and care settings, connecting data from different sources to give clinicians a more complete and cohesive understanding of a patient’s medical history.” — Michael J. Schlosser, MD, MBA, FAANS, Executive Vice President and Chief Clinical Officer, HCA Healthcare.

  • “Healthcare generates enormous amounts of information and data every day, yet patients often experience care as a series of separate interactions rather than one connected journey. Through our work with Google Cloud, we're exploring how AI can help connect information across the healthcare experience, making it easier to support the whole person, create more personalized care experiences, and equip clinicians with meaningful insights at the right time.” — Karen Hanlon, President, Highmark Health.

  • "By leveraging Gemini for healthcare, we will be able to use technology in a way that elevates the patient experience and strengthens the relationship between caregivers and those they serve. Through these integrated solutions, we expect to ease some of the administrative burden on our clinical teams and give them more time for what matters most: caring for their patients.
