title: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization
summary:
Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia.

Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows. Nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 are already using Gemini Enterprise to build, scale and govern agents. But as AI systems begin to plan, execute multi-step processes, and work alongside human teams, leaders are confronting this same tension between cutting-edge and legacy technology.

To understand how existing technology environments shape an organization’s ability to operationalize AI, Google Cloud partnered with Hypothesis Group to survey 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The findings reveal a critical paradox: the legacy software systems enterprises rely on to deliver technology to their employees are simultaneously functioning as an innovation tax, actively holding back the AI transformation leaders are trying to achieve.

Legacy IT’s operational toll

In our study, we defined “legacy” technology as software running locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud. Across industries, decision-makers report that maintaining this footprint exerts a constant friction on their AI ambitions.

The consequences to AI are not theoretical. Nearly half (49%) of respondents report that relying on on-premises software has actively delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives.

Digging deeper, routine patch application and maintenance emerged as a primary operational bottleneck. As AI-enabled vulnerability discovery accelerates, the rate at which flaws are surfaced in legacy codebases has outpaced what human security teams can realistically address.

This creates a zero-sum game between routine maintenance of legacy systems and AI modernization. Instead of directing engineer cycles toward AI modernization, IT teams are spending their time and resources on maintaining legacy systems.

Enterprise monoculture

Why do organizations continue to rely on legacy environments that constrain their modernization? As our research shows, it is not necessarily architectural preference — but the result of vendor lock-in.
 
Beyond narrowing technology choice, deep provider dependence introduces commercial constraints. In our study, 39% of decision-makers report that reliance on legacy software and cloud providers forces them to navigate complex licensing rules or contracts, or limited negotiating flexibility.
 
Even more concerning is the systemic operational risk created by single-vendor concentration. Concentrating operating systems, productivity applications, cloud hosting and emerging AI models within a single vendor's monoculture creates an immense single point of failure. An autonomous AI agent is only as secure as the operating system and network it traverses. When that underlying stack is vulnerable, organizations are not deploying resilient intelligence; they are expanding their attack surface.

Customer choice

The solution to vendor lock-in is straightforward: enterprise buyers and policymakers must ensure organizations have genuine choice and interoperability in their software, cloud and AI architectures.

Furthermore, 80% of leaders agree that a provider’s installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, while 78% believe that the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. Organizations want the freedom to choose best-of-breed intelligence on its own merits, rather than accepting bundled defaults tied to legacy desktop software.

Accelerate agentic technology

Delivering this level of autonomous agility across the enterprise requires modern technology built to support the agentic era. Here are a few ideas to get there:

  • Demand architectural and provider choice: AI and cloud must never be held hostage by the legacy software running local servers, email or desktop operating systems. Organizations need the commercial and architectural freedom to select best-of-breed IT on its own merits.
  • Commit to secure-by-design foundations: The industry must move past the broken cycle of releasing insecure software and patching it after the fact. Software manufacturers must engineer durable, resilient architectures where entire vulnerability classes are eliminated before code ever ships — relieving understaffed IT teams from perpetual applying routine but necessary patches.
  • Deploy AI-driven defense to remediate legacy debt: For the millions of lines of vulnerable legacy software already running in production, organizations must shift from manual triage to proactive, AI-assisted defense. By deploying platforms like Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics, teams can use intelligence to continuously surface active exploit paths, prioritize critical exposure and automate remediation across complex, hybrid environments.

The promise of agentic AI is to help automate friction away, and accelerate human ingenuity. But that future cannot be built on top of software designed decades ago. As IT leaders plan their roadmaps, it is time to ask: Is your technology foundation accelerating your future, or are you paying a maintenance tax just to keep the past running?

Learn more about the research here.

title: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs
summary:
Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. To help, dynamic slicing decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. GKE dynamic slicing is generally available.

Beyond one workload, one nodepool 

Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency. 

Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams:

  • Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted.

  • Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment.

  • Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable.

  • Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes. 

  • Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling.

Dynamic slicing architecture

GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube.

Dynamic super-slicing

GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency.

Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice.

Dynamic sub-slicing

Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy.

When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool.

Customer use cases

You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments.  

Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE 

GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation.

Getting started

Pre-provision nodepools

To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand. 

Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover.

This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes.

Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing 

After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations.

Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples.

Repair

When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies:

  • Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes.

  • Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions.

Next steps 

Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for  TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For  working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation.

title: The Blueprint: Orchestrating 5,000+ AI assets for a World Cup TV spot
summary:
Welcome back to The Blueprint, a regular feature where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

AI is rapidly transforming video production at virtually every step of the process, from ideation and storyboarding to filming, editing, and release. At Mito, we’re striving to democratize AI-powered video creation, enabling everyone from solo artists to large enterprises to get the most out of the best creative technologies available.

The Challenge

When we founded Mito, our goal was to eliminate the complex technical friction that stops creators from telling long-form, narrative stories with generative AI. 

However, transitioning from a single five-second clip to a cohesive campaign — such as a 120-second national TV spot for Movistar Plus+, a part of Telefónica, to broadcast across Spain during the World Cup this summer. This effort revealed massive infrastructure and workflow bottlenecks:

  • Asset & workflow overhead: Managing local media libraries across individual workstations was unscalable. For Movistar alone, our production required generating a massive "iceberg" of over 5000 assets (1000 of those videos) generated in around 65 iteration rounds.

  • Zero real-time collaboration: Traditional feedback loops required manual downloads, Google Drive uploads, and fragmented communication across chat apps and email.

  • Rendering latency: Standard AI video rendering takes four to five minutes per short clip. Running these processes synchronously froze our user interface and stalled creative velocity.

  • Model disparity & consistency: Every generative model requires distinct prompting logic. Maintaining character persistence, specific lighting, and camera angles across dozens of shots — while preserving the likeness of real public figures like chef Ferran Adrià or journalist Juanma Castaño — was nearly impossible without central orchestration.

  • Capacity constraints: Operating on public pay-as-you-go model APIs left us vulnerable to rate limits and regional throughput throttling during peak traffic.

The Solution

To deliver an infinite, real-time creative canvas for filmmakers, we designed a serverless, asynchronous architecture built on Google Cloud.

We run our API, AI Director, and background workers as Java services on Cloud Run, which scales with request volume.

In order to address message routing challenges, we decoupled job execution using Google Cloud Pub/Sub as our central event bus. Long-running video generations are offloaded to background Cloud Run workers, allowing creators to keep working uninterrupted on the UI canvas.

To minimize latency, media assets are stored in Google Cloud Storage and delivered via Cloud CDN. Expiring key signatures keep pre-release client assets strictly private. Keeping our storage alongside the models we call through Vertex AI reduces network transfer delays.

An isolated database architecture helps with the heavy business intelligence and analytics workloads while mitigating potential negative impacts on production performance through Cloud SQL and PostgreSQL. We rely heavily on foundational models like Omni, Veo and Nano Banana, which we access through Vertex AI alongside our custom system prompts.

Finally, our structured canvas frontend enforces a "Rule of 6" (limiting prompt variables across World, Camera, Light, Texture, Actions, and Character) and prioritizes still-frame generation before video rendering to maximize cost efficiency.

The Architecture

The Outcome

By pairing our creative orchestration platform with Google Cloud’s infrastructure, we successfully delivered a landmark national broadcast campaign that the production team describes as 95% AI-generated:

  • Prime-time scale: The 120-second Movistar campaign for the Spanish National Team  aired across every major television channel in Spain, with 1,441 assets live on a single shared Canvas near launch.

  • AI Director copilot: Our conversational agent translates natural language instructions into precise model parameters while maintaining context, lighting, and visual style across every scene.

  • Seamless collaboration: Distributed teams and brand clients can work on the same canvas in real time. Because new generations are saved as separate assets instead of overwriting earlier ones, stakeholders can duplicate projects to explore parallel creative ideas.

  • Continuous dogfooding: Through our internal studio, Mito Films, we put our tools to the test on high-stakes client projects — whether that's global television spots or keynotes for top robotics startups — ensuring direct feedback flows back into engineering.

  • Future-proof foundation: Our architecture is primed for rendering times to collapse from minutes to seconds, positioning Mito to handle upcoming world models, deeper memory states, and personalized content delivery.

The Details

Building an enterprise-grade platform for AI storytelling required solving several backend and creative challenges. This includes our creation of a virtual queuing system that mitigates third-party API rate limiting during usage spikes for smooth request concurrency, with bounded retries and a clear outcome for every job.

Because creative output cannot be fully validated with standard unit tests, we built an automated evaluation harness powered by Gemini. Acting as an independent judge, it evaluates AI Director outputs against original user intents across an automated test suite, which we run alongside standard tests for high-impact Director changes.

We knew early on that we would need multi-model intelligence routing. As such, we built the AI Director to dynamically coordinate tasks across multiple specialized models — including Sonnet, Gemini, and ElevenLabs for audio — treating the spatial canvas like a live code repository to infer adjacent contextual cues.

We also needed to embrace an “imperfect aesthetic” to arrive at a more authentic outcome. In our Movistar spot, the story follows Tommy, a 17-year-old student making an AI video project. At the climax, the AI misunderstands a prompt, making coach Luis de la Fuente say "In the same milkshake" while holding a drink. Tommy edits the prompt live to "In the same heartbeat," and the video recalibrates instantly. 

By incorporating surreal visual elements — like stadium stands built into Galician cliffs or a neighborhood bar covered in pitch grass — we showcased how generative AI can elevate human storytelling rather than obscure it.

title: Bringing conversational analytics to Gemini with Agentic Data Cloud connectors
summary:
Data Cloud connectors in Gemini for business, now in preview, give business users and analysts a direct way to query live enterprise data in natural language. Across most organizations, data questions multiply faster than analysts can answer them: Projects stall in ticket queues, leaders fall back on guesswork, and unmanaged spreadsheets spread across teams. Early generative AI tools promised conversational access to data, but they often struggled to generate accurate SQL across complex schemas or to respect governance rules. Data Cloud connectors let you query governed data directly from your workspace while enforcing row- and column-level security and respecting end-user credentials.

A new way to query enterprise data

Gemini brings conversational analytics directly into your day-to-day workflow through two paths: Conversational Analytics agents, which let you create data agents that include context and instructions to effectively answer questions for specific use cases, and Data Cloud connectors, allowing you to query live data directly with Gemini. End users can pull data directly from BigQuery (preview), operational databases like Spanner, AlloyDB, and Cloud SQL (preview), and governed data from Looker (preview). From there, you can move your findings directly into everyday tools, such as turning query results into a Google Doc, an email draft in Gmail, or a deck in Google Slides.

How Data Cloud connectors work

Data Cloud connectors work with Knowledge Catalog to locate relevant data, interpret your question, and execute permission-scoped queries under your identity.

When you ask a question in Gemini, the system coordinates discovery, semantic interpretation, and query execution, using the following capabilities:

  1. Natural-language question: You ask an exploratory question in plain language (for example, "How many sales did we have this month for all cold weather products?"). End users aren’t expected to know the table or project to use.

  2. Semantic discovery: Gemini searches Knowledge Catalog to locate candidate data across your estate, considering key attributes like usage patterns.

  3. Context mapping: The system uses technical metadata, business glossaries, and semantic models to map everyday terms into exact database structures, such as resolving "cold weather products" to specific categories like sweaters, coats, and jackets in an ecommerce catalog.

  4. Permission-aware execution: Gemini generates a SQL query and runs it through the connector under your user credentials, respecting your existing row- and column-level database permissions.

To accurately navigate an enterprise data estate, language models need business context alongside raw database access. Knowledge Catalog provides a curated context bundle, including technical metadata, business logic, table relationships, and verified queries, that improves query accuracy while reducing latency and token consumption.

Enterprise analytics has long been fragmented by physical borders: data locked in proprietary silos, open lakehouse tables in cloud object storage, and datasets distributed across multicloud environments. Beyond native BigQuery storage, the BigQuery connector brings conversational analytics to a borderless lakehouse, unifying these environments into a single conversational interface to query open table formats (including Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Parquet) and cross-cloud datasets in AWS or Azure using BigQuery. The connector inherits fine-grained access policies from BigQuery and Knowledge Catalog, so row- and column-level access controls apply whether you query native tables or open lakehouse files.

Choosing between connectors and data agents

In addition to using direct Data Cloud connectors to query data in plain language, you can also use Conversational Analytics agents to enable these experiences. While Data Cloud connectors allow you to provide exploratory and ad hoc analysis for users, conversational analytics agents are scoped agents that are built and certified directly by data teams within your organization. These can be built across Data Cloud products such as BigQuery, Looker, and operational databases including Spanner, AlloyDB, and Cloud SQL.

These pre-configured agents allow users to run highly governed, multi-step strategic analyses that are scoped to particular subsets of data, supporting compliance requirements and predictable results for reporting. These data agents can also be published in Gemini for consumption or made available via API for building your own conversational apps in the enterprise.

These approaches are complementary. Gemini direct connectivity also surfaces relevant published agents created by central data teams, so users can decide whether to proceed with ad hoc analysis using the connectors or use the scoped agent. You can choose the right approach for each workload.

Built-in access controls and governance

Data Cloud connector queries execute under the end user’s identity. An employee without access to executive salary data or protected healthcare records cannot query that data through natural-language prompts. The agent only discovers metadata in Knowledge Catalog to which you have access, and only executes queries that your account has permission to run.

How to create Data Cloud connectors

Administrators can configure Data Cloud connectors in the Gemini admin console. From there, admins set up default read-only connections to datasets in BigQuery, operational databases, or Looker, with Knowledge Catalog enabled automatically. Once configured, end users can enable the connector in Gemini to start querying data and building reports in plain language.

Setup documentation is available for the BigQuery, Spanner, Cloud SQL, and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connectors, with Looker also in preview.

Unlike data ingestion mode, which copies data into a Gemini data store, Data Cloud connectors use federated query mode to query your data in place without copying or indexing it — using Knowledge Catalog automatically to search accessible metadata and look up business context.

Why use Data Cloud connectors over custom MCP

Compared to connecting to public or self-managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, first-party Data Cloud connectors provide two main advantages:

  1. Built-in skills for higher response quality: Data Cloud connectors include pre-configured agent skills tailored to each data engine, such as advanced SQL and AI function generation for BigQuery and operational databases, to improve query accuracy and response quality.

  2. Guided setup and managed authentication: First-party connectors provide a guided setup experience with managed authentication for Google Cloud databases and BigQuery, removing the need to deploy MCP middleware or manage your own OAuth client configuration for Google Cloud services. In addition, connector-specific settings, such as specifying a default Google Cloud billing project for BigQuery query execution, help administrators enforce governance and manage query costs.

Get started today

Data Cloud connectors help teams find answers from enterprise data sources without waiting on backlog queues. To get started, review the Data Cloud connectors documentation or explore Conversational Analytics agents.

title: How Nammu21 automates syndicated loans on Google Cloud Universal Ledger
summary:
The syndicated loan and private credit markets, both critical components of corporate finance, have long been constrained by manual processes, leading to multi-week settlements, valuation opacity, and trade friction. 

To solve these long-standing challenges, fintech innovator Nammu21 partnered with Google Cloud on a new proof-of-concept. Using its AI-powered platform to structure legal agreements and instantiate them as smart contracts on the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL), Nammu21 automates the entire loan lifecycle, paving the way for improved settlement times and greater market efficiency.

Digitizing the loan market

While loan markets provide billions in capital to businesses worldwide, their underlying infrastructure has not kept pace with the speed of digital finance. This landscape requires continuous coordination across facility agents, borrowers, and diverse lender syndicates, while also managing highly customized credit agreements with dynamic tranches and complex covenants. 

In particular, relying on fragmented, manual interpretation of legal text often results in significant operational drag and data silos. According to the Loan Market Association, secondary market settlement times for par/near par loans in Q4 2024 still averaged 42 days, with a median of 27 days. These notoriously slow timelines tie up capital, increase counterparty risk, and create a heavy reconciliation burden for participants.

Nammu21 transforms bespoke credit documents into programmable assets at scale by rendering each facility's governing terms as a Digital Credit Instrument (DCI). The DCI maps every term — including conditions, consents, eligibility criteria, and operational mechanics that determine what is permitted under a facility — directly back to its originating legal provision. These elements are then expressed as executable behaviours against a loan's live state. 

To instantiate these instruments, the proof-of-concept utilizes the secure, high-performance execution environment of GCUL, an institutional-grade, permissioned distributed ledger that helps automate complex financial workflows to deliver near-instant transaction finality and predictable costs without the volatility or security concerns of public blockchains.

A purpose-built stack for digital credit

Combined with Nammu21’s data intelligence, GCUL provides the foundational infrastructure for converting legal document logic into live, programmable contracts. Designed to handle the privacy, scale, and multi-party coordination required by institutional finance, GCUL provides a permissioned, high-performance distributed ledger that delivers deterministic, instant transaction finality for high-value financial settlements.

Programmable contracts on GCUL are written in gculpy, GCUL's domain-optimized programming language. As a strict, statically-typed subset of Python, gculpy is designed to be safe, readable, and auditable, making it ideal for processing complex financial logic.

For regulated financial institutions, gculpy offers distinct operational advantages over other ledger programming models. The language simplifies development by removing the need for complex memory management or workarounds to meet highly restrictive call stack limits, allowing engineers to focus on the financial logic itself. 

GCUL also provides robust, built-in permissioning, requiring explicit user authorization before a contract can store data on their behalf. This solves the "unsolicited asset" problem — common on public networks — where unwanted tokens can be sent to an organization's wallet, creating compliance and accounting issues. With GCUL, institutions can maintain full control over which assets they interact with to support their high-value, highly regulated use cases.

Nammu21 serves a dual role in this architecture. First, the platform renders the DCI programmatically from the original legal agreement without manual document reading to establish the terms. Next, it derives gculpy contracts that define the structure of the obligation and govern the loan on GCUL, using the DCI to supply the terms that determine what the loan documents permit, require and block.

Technical architecture: The loan lifecycle on GCUL

Nammu21’s loan implementation on GCUL demonstrates the value of creating a single, immutable source of truth. The proof-of-concept modeled a $1.945 billion Term Loan B — one segment of a broader multi-facility transaction — where the agent bank, borrower, transferor, and transferee all worked off a permissioned view of the same on-ledger rendering.

The lifecycle begins when an agent bank selects a specific credit agreement transformed by Nammu21. The platform instantly provides the structured terms from the document, which are used to instantiate a unique gculpy contract on GCUL, establishing a verifiable, on-ledger digital twin of that specific loan facility.

Next, the agent bank initiates the onboarding of the borrower and lenders. This multilateral action requires that each participant review the request and then provide explicit consent by approving the onboarding invitation from their own interface. Once all parties are onboarded, the agent bank records an immutable hash of the loan's key terms on-ledger, attesting that the on-ledger data matches the canonical off-ledger records.

Subsequent lifecycle events, such as secondary market transfers or repayments, are also managed as multi-step, automated workflows governed by a consent-driven model. For example, a transfer of a loan position requires new lender, borrower, and agent bank consent  before it can be executed atomically on the ledger. All payment flows, from interest payments to loan close-outs, settle directly on GCUL using tokenized commercial bank money, eliminating the need for external payment rails.

Transacting with familiar, regulated money on a programmable ledger provides an architecture purpose-built for institutional finance, grounded in three core pillars:

1. Compliance via gated execution: Nammu21’s gculpy contracts instantiated with governing terms, validate every action against the terms transformed from the agreement before execution, mitigating potential covenant breaches or invalid transfers upfront while eliminating the risk of silent failures. 

2. Role-based privacy: GCUL enforces strict, role-based access, ensuring that trading strategies, positions, and sensitive loan data remain confidential and are visible only to the necessary counterparties in a transaction.

3. Settlement finality: Every on-ledger action completes near-instantly and anchors on canonical data derived from the original credit agreement, replacing provisional, reconciliation-heavy models with real-time, trusted verification.

The business impact of moving on-ledger

This proof-of-concept illustrates a structural shift in how credit markets can operate. When each facility's governing terms are rendered as a DCI and executed on GCUL, the operational mechanics of lending markets change fundamentally, rather than incrementally. 

Values can be reconciled bilaterally, but governance logic cannot – and the market’s current friction stems directly from each party's independent interpretation of the rules. Resolving this issue on-ledger is what enables settlement times to compress, back-office overhead to shrink, and counterparty risk to be mitigated by design rather than by manual checking. 

This same architecture can be applied wherever credit terms are bespoke and manually interpreted. By freeing up capital that would otherwise be trapped in lengthy settlement cycles, new liquidity is unlocked and a more dynamic and efficient secondary loan market can emerge.

The team would also like to thank Someera Khokhar, Jordan Shelley, and Saskia A. Aalders at Nammu21 and Googlers Ishan Singh, Kathryn Stavish, Tom Chudy, and Stathis Onasoglou for their contributions.

title: Introducing Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam for agents
summary:
Authors: Burak Gokturk, VP Research & Development; Rujun Han, Research Scientist; George Lee, Product Manager.

Today, the Google AI & Infrastructure team is announcing Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE), a new benchmark and open competition, developed in collaboration with Mercor, and built to test a frontier model’s ability to complete tasks in mechanical, electrical, civil and structural engineering. 

To help the research community measure and improve how agents handle physical engineering work, we are releasing 29 public tasks, their grading tools, and an open competition leaderboard at ple-bench.com.

Frontier labs and the broader research community use model examinations to test AI’s progress in completing tasks in a specific discipline. Humanity's Last Exam measures a model’s general knowledge. Agents' Last Exam measures a model’s ability to complete digital professional work. Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE) measures a model’s ability to complete work that helps build the physical world. Physical engineers design skyscrapers, power grids, and computer chips we rely on, yet we could find no existing benchmark that tests whether frontier models can do that work end to end.

Why textbook benchmarks fall short for physical engineering

Frontier language models now score above 90% on many academic benchmarks. However, those benchmarks mostly test textbook-style questions, single tool calls, or small, self-contained design problems. For AI developers and researchers building agents for physical  engineering, existing benchmarks do not show whether an agent can produce safe, code-compliant, and cost-effective designs under a licensed engineer's review and control. As the demand for infrastructure development outpaces financing, there is a growing opportunity for agents to support engineers working to close this gap.   

Inside PLE: Real-world tasks built with practicing engineers

PLE closes this evaluation gap with 85 long-horizon tasks across four core disciplines: mechanical (30 tasks), electrical (27 tasks), civil (18 tasks), and structural (10 tasks) engineering.

Instead of answering a single prompt, an agent works inside a containerized project folder — built on Mercor’s Archipelago environment — that mirrors what a practicing engineer receives on the job. Each task holds an average of 61 files (5,170 total files across the benchmark), including PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, 2D CAD drawings, 3D BIM models, and document revisions. The agent must reason through these files, find the governing building codes and physical limits, run calculations, and generate production-ready deliverables that a licensed reviewer would review and approve.

In collaboration with experts from Mercor and licensed practicing engineers from industry, we built PLE using two methods:

  • Expert-authored tasks (44 tasks): Practicing engineers created the project folders, prompts, and grading rubrics based on real professional engineering tasks.

  • Co-authored tasks (41 tasks): Practicing engineers designed the initial task and an agent pipeline assembled the task's environment and grader from licensable engineering standards. Engineers then validated and increased the difficulty of every task assembled by the agent.

All frontier models score below 50%

We tested 14 frontier models on PLE using seven publicly available agent harnesses (Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenHands, and Pi). Because PLE evaluates both code compliance and cost efficiency, agents only earn points if their design passes every hard safety check first. Our baseline results show a wide gap between current models and real-world engineering requirements:

  • High headroom: All frontier models score below 50% on our private test set, with the highest-performing model on its native harness reaching a mean score of 48.3%.

  • Hard safety gates: While the top-scoring agent configuration satisfied 91% of individual constraints on co-authored tasks, only 41.3% of its deliverables passed every hard safety and feasibility check required.

  • Model vs. harness impact: Choice of model drives performance far more than the harness (up to a 50-point spread across models, versus a median 3-point spread across harnesses for the same model), though harnesses significantly affect run cost.

Test your agent and join the open competition

Evaluating AI agents on realistic project files, strict safety rules, and material costs is a practical step toward building helpful tools for physical engineers. Here is how you can get started with PLE today:

  • Check out the full technical breakdown in our PLE paper on arXiv.

  • Download the 29 public tasks, grading scripts, and evaluation container from our GitHub repository.

  • Bring your own agent setup and submit it for evaluation on our private test set at ple-bench.com—with 13 Google-sponsored models running free on our servers and prize details coming soon.

These integrations enable your agents to retrieve data and execute tasks with your systems-of-record. 

3. AI Hypercomputer: Designed specifically for demanding AI workloads, our AI Hypercomputer is an advanced, purpose-built architecture that unites performance-optimized hardware for compute, storage, networking, open software and machine learning frameworks — as well as flexible consumption models — into a single, integrated system. We are announcing innovations at every layer of the AI Hypercomputer:

  • TPU 8t, optimized for training, uses breakthrough Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) technology to scale up to 9,600 TPUs and 2 PB of shared, high-bandwidth memory in a single superpod. It achieves 3x the processing power of Ironwood and delivers up to 2x more performance/Watt. 
  • TPU 8i, optimized for inference, uses our new Boardfly topology to directly connect 1,152 TPUs in a single pod. It features 3x more on-chip SRAM compared to previous versions to host larger KV caches entirely on-silicon and integrates a specialized Collectives Acceleration Engine. Taken together, TPU 8i delivers 80% better performance per dollar for inference than the prior generation, enabling millions of concurrent agents to run cost-effectively.

4. The Agentic Data Cloud: A new data architecture built for the speed and scale of agentic AI. The Agentic Data Cloud delivers an AI-native architecture, allowing agents to perceive, reason, and act on your behalf in real-time, including: 

  • Cross-Cloud Lakehouse, standardized on Apache Iceberg, is our Lakehouse that enables you to leave your data in AWS or Azure (coming later this year) while querying it instantly — without the friction of vendor lock-in or the cost of data movement

  • Knowledge Catalog constructs a unified, dynamic context graph of your entire business enabling you to ground agents in all of your business data and semantics. With Smart Storage and the Object Context API, files in Google Cloud Storage are instantly tagged and enriched with metadata before an agent touches them. Then our Knowledge Engine uses Gemini to autonomously tag, define logic and instantly map complex relationships across your entire enterprise, providing the semantic definition your agents have been missing. 

5. Protecting the agentic enterprise: Security built for the AI era. Our full-stack AI approach, from the chips to the models, gives you a competitive advantage with better integration and velocity to help protect customers. Not only can Google action insights from the world’s largest threat observatory and Mandiant frontline experts, but we also bring cutting-edge insights and breakthroughs from Google DeepMind, to help make your platforms more secure.

  • Agentic defense: Three new agents in Google Security Operations can help hunt threats, engineer detections, and provide context on third parties. You can build your own security agents with remote Google Cloud model context protocol (MCP) server support for Google Security Operations, now generally available. You can also access the MCP server client directly from the Google Security Operations chat interface, available in preview.
  • Protecting AI and cloud apps across any infrastructure with Wiz: Newly expanded AI coverage helps build secure agents across clouds and AI studios. New AI-Bill of Materials in development tools can help secure AI-generated code and mitigate the risk of shadow AI. Learn more.
  • Securing agents and the agentic web: Model Armor can integrate with Agent Gateway, and new Agent Identities provide more layers of defense against shadow AI. Google Cloud Fraud Defense, the next evolution of reCAPTCHA, offers agent-specific capabilities that can help secure the agentic web as well as the entire user and customer journey.   
  • Trusted Cloud: We’re simplifying permissions with modern IAM, and advancing Google Cloud security with new capabilities in Security Command Center plus new innovations in data and network security.
  • New partner-supported workflows for Google Security Operations: This new robust cohort of partner integrations includes partners developing their own agentic security operations centers (SOCs).

You can catch up on all our security announcements from Next ‘26 here. 

News you can use 

  • Guide to prompting Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS (text-to-speech): The new TTS model introduces a high level of controllability by allowing you to steer the delivery using more than 200 audio tags. We'll share how to get strong results from the model, whether you are building accessible gaming soundtracks, banking systems, or audiobooks. Learn more about the model here. 

  • Ultimate prompting guide for Lyria 3 models: Lyria 3, Google's family of music-generation models, is designed to give you granular control over vocals, instrumentation, and arrangement. So we spent weeks testing against every musical genre and use case we could imagine. We put together this guide to share exactly what we learned and how you can get the best results.

  • How to find the sweet spot between cost and performance: This guide will walk you through Google Cloud's flexible gen AI infrastructure options, showing you how to find that sweet spot on the efficient frontier between cost and performance. We'll start with the foundational pay-as-you-go (PayGo) models and then explore how to layer on more specialized options to build a robust and cost-effective gen AI strategy.

  • Essential AI and cloud security now on by default: To support the next generation of AI innovators, we are offering on by default essential AI security and cloud security in Security Command Center Standard.

  • Cloud CISO Perspectives: AI, security, and the workforce of the future: You can’t bring traditional security to an AI fight, so how do we defend against AI-powered attacks, boost defenders with AI, and secure AI use? Drop in on this RSA Conference fireside chat between Francis deSouza, Google Cloud COO and President, Security Products, and Nick Godfrey, senior director, Office of the CISO.

March

March was a busy month for our AI teams. We launched Gemini Embedding 2, rolled out a highly cost-effective Veo 3.1 Lite model, and officially welcomed the Wiz team to Google Cloud to help redefine security in the AI era. 

Alongside these launches, we created comprehensive guides to help you get the most out of these models, from prompting formulas for Nano Banana 2, to practical advice for optimizing your TPU training. Here’s a quick look at the latest news and resources to help your team build what’s next.

Top hits: 

  • Gemini Embedding 2: Our first natively multimodal embedding model: Gemini Embedding 2 is our first natively multimodal embedding model that maps text, images, video, audio and documents into a single embedding space, enabling multimodal retrieval and classification across different types of media — and it’s available now in public preview.
  • Build with Veo 3.1 Lite, our most cost-effective video generation model: This model empowers developers to build high-volume video applications, at less than 50% of the cost of Veo 3.1 Fast, but with the same speed. This rounds out the Veo 3.1 model family, giving developers flexibility based on needs. For Cloud customers, it’s now available on Vertex AI. 

Here’s a fun bonus: Check out our ultimate prompting guide for Veo 3.1 to get started.

The Wiz team will join Google Cloud, and we will retain the Wiz brand. With the addition of Wiz, we will provide customers with a comprehensive platform to secure their cloud and hybrid environments, as well as accelerate threat prevention, detection, and response.
  • Gemini 3.1 Flash Live: Making audio AI more natural and reliable: We’ve improved 3.1 Flash Live’s overall quality, making it more reliable for developers and enterprises to build voice-first agents that can complete complex tasks at scale. On ComplexFuncBench Audio, a benchmark that captures multi-step function calling with various constraints, it leads with a score of 90.8% compared to our previous model.

News you can use:

Check out the guide to learn more.

In February, we’re giving developers more reasoning power with Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude 4.6, and faster creative scaling with Nano Banana 2. We’re also opening up new training programs and step-by-step guides to help you tackle the hardest parts of the AI lifecycle, from capacity planning to mounting defenses against AI-powered attacks.

Here’s a rundown of our latest news, tools, and resources to help you build what’s next.

Gemini 3.1 Pro is available starting today in preview in Vertex AI and Gemini Enterprise. Developers can access the model in preview via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, Android Studio, Google Antigravity, and Gemini CLI.

These resources first appeared during Kaggle’s 5 days of AI Agents Intensive, and they’ve proven so popular and useful, we wanted to make sure a wider audience had access, as well.

As a new specialized pathway within the Google Developer Program, GEAR empowers developers and pros to build and deploy enterprise-grade agents with Google AI.

Janurary

We used to have to learn the language of computers. In 2026, they’re learning ours.

We kicked off the year by exploring the future of agentic commerce, where AI agents navigate the web to find and buy products for us. Our leaders call this the "invisible shelf" — a world where commerce isn't tied to a specific website. To make this reality scalable, we announced the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), a shared language that allows agents and retailers to understand each other. 

We brought that same fluency to our creative and technical tools:

  1. Updates to Veo 3.1 allow creators to use simple inputs — like reference images — to generate precise, mobile-ready video.

  2. Natural language queries: With Comments to SQL in BigQuery, we’re removing the language barrier to data. Engineers can now write queries by describing their intent in natural language, prioritizing the question over the code.

Let’s dive in.

Top hits 

1. Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience (CX): Specifically built for agentic retail, this platform transforms fragmented search, commerce and service touch points into one seamless journey — whether you need a shopping assistant, a support bot, agentic search or help with merchandising. 

2. We announced Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP): A new open standard for agentic commerce that works across the entire shopping journey — from discovery and buying to post-purchase support. UCP establishes a common language for agents and systems to operate together across consumer surfaces, businesses and payment providers. So instead of requiring unique connections for every individual agent, UCP enables all agents to interact easily. UCP is built to work across verticals and is compatible with existing industry protocols like Agent2Agent (A2A), Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) and Model Context Protocol (MCP).

3. We updated Veo 3.1, including improvements to Ingredients to Video and Portrait mode: Veo is getting more expressive, with improvements that help you create more fun, creative, high-quality videos based on ingredient images, built directly for the mobile format. This includes:

  • Improvements to Veo 3.1 Ingredients to Video, our capability that lets you create videos based on reference images. 

  • Native vertical outputs for Ingredients to Video (portrait mode) to power mobile-first, short-form video creation.

  • State-of-the-art upscaling to 1080p and 4K resolution 1 for high-fidelity production workflows.

These updates are launching in the Gemini app, YouTube, Flow, Google Vids, the Gemini API and Vertex AI.

4. Vibe querying with comments-to-SQL: Crafting complex SQL queries can be challenging. Often, engineers simply want to express their data needs in plain English directly within their SQL workflow. That’s why we’re introducing Comments to SQL in BigQuery. This feature makes writing queries using natural language – ‘vibe querying’ – a reality. Learn more in the blog.

News you can use

Mastering Gemini CLI: Your complete guide from installation to advanced use-cases: We’ve teamed up with DeepLearning.ai and are excited to announce a free course – Gemini CLI: Code & Create with an Open-Source Agent. This course isn’t just for developers; we dive into practical use cases for various tasks such as data analysis, content creation, and personalized learning.
  2. How Google SREs use Gemini CLI to solve real-world outages: In this article, we’ll delve into real scenarios that Google SREs are solving today using Gemini 3 (our latest foundation model) and Gemini CLI—the go-to tool for bringing agentic capabilities to the terminal.

Getting started with Gemini 3: Deploy your first Gemini 3 app to Google Cloud Run: In this blog, we will show you how to vibe code your first app—which leverages the Gemini 3 Flash Preview model and deploy it as a publicly accessible URL on Google Cloud Run. Google AI Studio lets you go from idea to app quickly by using natural language to generate fully functional apps using the power of Gemini 3.

Practical guidance: Building with the Secure AI Framework (SAIF) on Google Cloud: We know that security and data privacy are the top concern for executives when evaluating AI providers, and security is the top use case for AI agents in a majority of industries. To help you build AI boldly and responsibly, here’s our guide to developing AI with the Secure AI Framework (SAIF) on Google Cloud.

title: Innovate on your own business terms: Google Cloud spend caps now generally available
summary:
Today, we’re announcing that spend caps on Google Cloud Budgets are generally available. 

With this release, we’re delivering ways to protect your workloads from runaway costs without risking resource deletion. More importantly, we’re introducing three major updates, directly inspired by your feedback since the initial preview, to bring programmability, real-time visibility, and automated guardrails to your cost-control playbook.

How the new spend caps can help your business 

We have significantly enhanced the usability and power of spend caps in three ways: 

1. Automation through spend caps API: Managing guardrails manually across hundreds of projects is a major operational challenge. To address this, we have launched the spend caps API, which can be accessed from the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API. You can now programmatically enforce your financial boundaries for eligible services within each project, without additional overhead. You can automatically lift, update, or delete caps on the fly and instantly apply a spend cap whenever a developer spins up a new sandbox project.

2. Real-time visibility with live cost reports: Spend caps for AI services trigger within minutes of usage using estimated, live costs. When a cap triggers, you need to know exactly why and when the limit was breached. You can now view these faster, estimated costs directly inside your Cost Reports. Instead of waiting hours for standard billing pipelines to settle net costs, you get the exact financial snapshots that triggered the enforcement, giving you the immediate context needed to run a precise root-cause analysis.

3. Automated guardrails for your monthly resets: Before, once a spend cap was triggered, the usage block remained locked until you manually lifted it in the UI. Today, we are introducing automated monthly resets. You no longer need to worry about manually lifting caps every month. Enforced spend caps will automatically reset, and blocked services will seamlessly resume at the beginning of the next month. However, if your governance policies require a strict manual audit before resuming operations, the manual override option continues to exist exactly as before. 

Best practices for deploying spend caps

As you roll out spend caps across your organization, keep these operational tips in mind:

  1. Target non-production environments first: Start by applying strict, low-dollar spend caps to your developer sandboxes, testing clusters, and experimental AI agent playgrounds.
  2. Configure alerts wisely: Default alerts are automatically sent to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the cap. Make sure the right folks are set up in these roles. This ensures your team is never caught off guard when a budget is nearing depletion. Spend caps permissions can also be added to custom roles, if needed.  
  3. Understand fixed vs on-demand costs: Spend caps halt pay-as-you-go and CUD-covered requests once the budget threshold is hit. However, Provisioned Throughput is never halted; requests using reserved capacity will continue to run, and serve traffic normally.

Refresher on GCP’s dual-pronged defense playbook

Spend Caps work seamlessly alongside our native Early Anomalies Detection to provide a closed-loop defense for your cloud spend. Read our previous blog for a detailed explanation on how to use these tools to effortlessly set up a GCP defense playbook.

title: What’s new in AI infrastructure and orchestration in October
summary:
The Google Cloud AI Infrastructure team had another busy month in October, filled with new product launches and updates to power today’s AI and agentic workloads scalably and efficiently. We were also honored to share our progress with customers, partners, and the broader community at leading industry events, including NVIDIA GTC, PyTorch Conference, and AGNTCon + MCPCon. Let’s dive in!

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability.

  • AI Hypercomputer updates: At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 we announced updates to our agentic infrastructure, including to A5X instances powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, Virgo Network scale-out fabric, and Managed Lustre storage. These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently.

  • GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE, in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs.

  • GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters.

  • Modernization tools: Together at last. Google Cloud Modernize brings Google Cloud’s migration and modernization tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization and our new EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent, into a single portfolio. Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization.

  • Cloud Run product update: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run automatically scale worker pools based on Temporal task queue demands and scale down to zero when idle. This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: llm-d 1.0 is an open-source, Kubernetes-native serving stack that turns a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool, unifying distributed LLM inference across mixed Google Cloud TPU and GPU fleets. Co-founded by Google and partners, it provides production-ready benefits such as cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offloading, and priority-based flow control to dramatically improve context reuse, reduce time-to-first-token latency, and efficiently scale multi-tenant agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: Working with Meta, we open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack that integrates Google TPUs directly into the PyTorch ecosystem alongside GPUs and CPUs. Now developers can train, serve, and deploy models natively on TPUs using familiar frameworks like Hugging Face, vLLM, and TorchTitan.

  • Google Distributed Cloud updates: Organizations that operate under strict sovereignty mandates would love to use AI to help them process data, but can’t send it to the cloud. The latest version of Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped brings frontier AI models and multimodal enterprise search with Gemini into these isolated environments. In addition, GDC air-gapped supports NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture, and features enhanced networking and security capabilities. 

  • Edge inference product: Google open-sourced ML Drift, a cross-platform on-device GPU compute engine built for LiteRT that abstracts hardware complexities across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU. The framework delivers peak performance, enhanced 5D tensor support, and memory efficiency for both classical machine learning workloads and advanced generative AI models at the edge.

  • Open-weight model support: Reflection's Beam is an open-weight, 501-parameter model released under an Apache 2.0 license designed specifically for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. We announced day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for service Beam on AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • AI network reference architectures: In Networking for AI inference model serving - GKE only and for all other backends, learn about reference architectures for AI inference model serving that provide centralized governance and private IP routing using Private Service Connect, Apigee API Management, and Model Armor. These architectures simplify multi-model scaling and prompt security across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid clouds. 

  • How-to guide: A Tale of TPU Observability on GKE: Part 2 - Dynamic Slicing Enhancements breaks down GKE's new Dynamic Slicing observability tools and metrics for next-generation v7 TPUs through an engaging, story-driven observability guide featuring Alex, a lead AI platform engineer. Explore the step-by-step diagnostic workflows with real-world examples and handy command-line snippets. Check out Part 1 here.

Customer and partner updates

  • AI21 achieves an 83% reduction in time-to-start for AI workloads with AI Hypercomputer: Frontier lab AI21 needed a new stack on which to train its Jamba family, and chose AI Hypercomputer configured with GKE on A3 and A3 Ultra instances. By doing so, AI21 says it cut high-priority job wait times from 72 hours to 12, and manual scheduling interventions from 20 per week to zero.

  • Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs: Visko, an AI startup developing interactive world models, deployed an end-to-end live inference pipeline that combines video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio onto a single Cloud TPU slice. In this blog, the team discusses how it engineered the pipeline, the architectural optimizations it made, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI.

  • ZenteiQ scales physical AI inference 4x with GKE and llm-d: In order to pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, Indian AI startup ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. GKE and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators.

  • Palo Alto Networks modernizes cloud-delivered security service: Palo Alto has worked with Google Cloud since 2018 to deliver its Prisma Access security service, and it was time to update it. In order not to compromise its security guarantees, Palo Alto separated the platform into two independently scalable layers: an ingress layer that handles traffic routing and forwarding running on GKE, with Axion C4A instances; and a security layer that handles threat inspection, running on dedicated single-tenant VMs fronted by an Internal Load Balancer. Each layer can now scale, update, and operate independently. 

  • Oracle is the first hyperscaler to provide TPUs outside Google Cloud: By deploying Google TPUs, Oracle is broadening the range of AI chips available through its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and giving customers more options for running AI workloads. Google TPUs on OCI will be available in 2027.

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • New resource: As enterprise organizations shift from isolated AI experiments to production-scale systems, different departments — from engineering and finance to executive leadership — often speak different technical dialects; The Encyclopedia of AI Infrastructure bridges that communication gap by demystifying complex infrastructure jargon.

  • Analyst report: We are thrilled to announce that Google was named a Leader in the inaugural 2026 IDC MarketScape for Agentic AI Platforms. 

  • Deep dive: A companion technical guide describing the architecture of Agent Compute Engine and how Google’s Gemini team needed both the isolation of a VM and the speed and density of a container to deliver personal agents for every Gemini user.

September 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

Google Kubernetes Engine updates: The GKE team is all about improving the scalability of the platform, and in September, those improvements came in many shapes and sizes:

  • New feature: Need an execution runtime with higher density for your agentic workloads? We engineered the new open-source GKE Agent Substrate to run millions of sandboxes with 10x higher density than standard container runtimes. Agent Substrate also delivers sub-500ms resume operations at over 500 suspend/resume activations per second with a native zero-trust kernel and network isolation. 

  • Product update: GKE now has scale-to-zero capabilities built-in. No need to configure complex components to scale your workloads down, thanks to the HPA with the Autoscaling Metric and support for KEP-2021, which do the job for you, out of the box. Read the blog to learn more. 

  • Product update: Further, the GKE HPA (with the above-mentioned Autoscaling Metric) now lets you scale up and down based on custom PromQL metrics, in addition to standard metrics, allowing you to trigger workloads according to conditions that are meaningful and unique to your business. Read more here. 

  • New feature: Yet another scalability feature is GKE Pod snapshots, which lets you save the running state of your workload, including CPU and GPU memory, and restore it on demand. According to internal tests, GKE Pod snapshots can reduce AI inference start-up by as much as 89%. Learn more here.

  • New migration tool: Finally, if you’ve always wanted to migrate your container workloads from AWS EKS to GKE but feared a daunting, high-friction engineering endeavor, we’ve just launched GKE agentic migration, a purpose-built agent plugin that replaces brittle, ad-hoc prompting with an AI-assisted migration pipeline protected by deterministic guardrails. Designed as a compilation of agent skills and a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, it uses AI to translate complex AWS EKS IaC and Kubernetes manifests directly into GKE landing zones. Get started with the onboarding guide.

  • Feature updates: Reinforcement learning (RL) and evaluation workloads are a beast: In a standard agentic RL loop, an LLM policy generates actions like code snippets on GPUs and executes them inside isolated CPU sandboxes to observe a reward signal. However, when scaling up this loop to support tens of thousands of parallel rollouts, infrastructure bottlenecks emerge, for instance idle accelerators, image cardinality, and a saturated control plane. To help, we developed GKE Agent Sandbox optimized for RL, plus an Agent Sandbox RL orchestration SDK and native integrations for popular RL gyms and harnesses. All are now generally available, and you can learn more here.

Storage updates: AI trains and creates lots of data, and that data has to live somewhere — in block storage systems, file systems, object stores and databases. We announced enhancements to our storage portfolio to help this critical layer roll with the agentic punches:  

  • Product update: Filestore agent volumes offer high-performance, elastic, persistent file storage for agentic workloads. Thanks to its tight integration with GKE Agent Substrate and GKE Agent Sandbox, Filestore agent volumes automatically allocates and attaches a dedicated, isolated file workspace to GKE agent sandboxes in milliseconds. Request access to the preview here. 

  • New product: If you run generative AI and RAG data layers  — think Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Vespa, Redis, and in-memory context caching — you may want to take a look at the M4N family of VMs, now GA, which offers the highest per-core IOPS and throughput of leading hyperscalers. Paired with Google Cloud's custom Titanium offload architecture and paired with Hyperdisk Extreme, M4N instances deliver up to 25,000 MiB/s (25 GiB/s) of aggregate host storage performance and up to 1 million IOPS. 

  • New product: Another new Compute Engine product, Z4D, is GA, and a strong storage solution for AI/ML training and inference workloads. When configured as a bare metal instance, Z4D provides both the high local SSD (LSSD) capacity and low latency required by agentic microVMs, so you can run thousands of isolated sandboxes per host with native performance and efficiency. Learn about Z4D machines here.
